_meta.note: Commodity reference sheet. Structure adapted from the Commodities 101 fact-sheet breakdown, with an India hedgeability layer added. Shares are indicative and dated - verify against the cited source before client-facing use. These are reference facts and are deliberately separate from the scoring array in index.html (DATA.commodities), which is what the risk models consume.

hedgeScale.4: Listed contract available onshore in INR (MCX / NCDEX) and liquid globally. Hedge onshore, no FX leg, lightest permission burden.
hedgeScale.3: Liquid listed contract exists offshore in USD only (LME / CME / ICE / SGX / DCE). Hedging needs an offshore commodity derivative under the RBI Master Direction plus an FX leg - and the FX leg is itself constrained by the April 2026 NDF prohibition.
hedgeScale.2: Listed but thin, or hedgeable only through a correlated proxy contract. Material basis risk; Ind AS 109 hedge effectiveness is hard to pass at 80-125%.
hedgeScale.1: No exchange contract. OTC swap, index-linked supply contract or formula pricing only. Counterparty credit and disclosure burden sit with the client.
hedgeScale.0: No financial hedge exists. Managed contractually only: pass-through clauses, indexation, tenders, inventory policy, dual sourcing.

gold.hook: India's second-largest import line after crude, and after the May 2026 duty hike the most policy-exposed price on the board.

trade.bench: LBMA Gold Price PM (USD/oz); COMEX GC front month
trade.lot: 100 oz (COMEX); 1 kg (MCX Gold); 8 g (MCX Gold Petal)
trade.terms: USD per troy ounce; INR per 10 g on MCX
trade.settle: LBMA loco London unallocated transfer; COMEX physical into approved vaults; MCX physical delivery at Ahmedabad
trade.curve: Contango set by the USD lease/forward rate (GOFO); backwardation is rare and signals physical stress
trade.liq: Deepest precious metal market; 24-hour OTC plus three liquid futures venues

ind.contract: MCX Gold (1 kg), Gold Mini (100 g), Gold Petal (1 g), Gold Guinea (8 g) - INR per 10 g, physically settled
ind.basis: MCX = LBMA x USDINR x (1 + import duty) + local premium/discount. The 13 May 2026 duty hike from 6% to 15% (10% BCD + 5% AIDC) repriced this basis by ~9 percentage points in one session, which is exactly the kind of move that breaks a hedge ratio set on the old duty. Duty is a policy variable, not a market one, and no listed instrument hedges it.
ind.note: India imports ~800 t/yr against negligible domestic mine output. Gold-on-lease funding used by jewellers carries a separate lease-rate exposure that the metal hedge does not cover.

drv: Real US yields and Fed path
Central bank buying, led by emerging Asia
Indian and Chinese physical demand and the festival/wedding calendar
Indian import duty and any policy aimed at the current account
gold.src: World Gold Council, USGS MCS 2026, LBMA, CBIC notification of 13 May 2026
gold.concWhy: Mine supply is fragmented; India's exposure is price and duty, not supply availability

silver.hook: Half precious metal, half industrial input - and the solar build-out has made the industrial half the marginal buyer.

trade.bench: LBMA Silver Price (USD/oz); COMEX SI
trade.lot: 5,000 oz (COMEX); 30 kg (MCX Silver), 5 kg (Silver Mini), 1 kg (Silver Micro)
trade.terms: USD per troy ounce; INR per kg on MCX
trade.settle: LBMA loco London; COMEX and MCX physical delivery
trade.curve: Usually contango; far more volatile than gold, roughly 1.5-2x gold's realised vol
trade.liq: Liquid but thinner than gold; prone to squeezes because visible above-ground stock is small relative to turnover

ind.contract: MCX Silver (30 kg), Silver Mini (5 kg), Silver Micro (1 kg) - INR per kg
ind.basis: Same duty-driven basis as gold: silver was included in the 13 May 2026 hike to 15%. Solar-cell and contact-paste importers carry the duty risk without the jewellery channel's ability to reprice.
ind.note: Hindustan Zinc is a material domestic by-product producer, which makes it one of the few Indian names that is long silver rather than short it.

Mine supply, most of which is a by-product of lead-zinc and copper mining and does not respond to the silver price

pallad.hook: A single Russian producer sets the marginal tonne of the metal in every petrol autocatalyst.

trade.bench: NYMEX PA front month; LBMA/LPPM palladium fix
trade.settle: Physical delivery into approved vaults; most industrial purchase is direct from refiners on formula pricing
trade.curve: Erratic; deep backwardation during the 2020-2022 supply squeeze
trade.liq: Thin. Small market, few participants, and a bid-ask that widens sharply in stress

ind.contract: No MCX contract. NYMEX only, USD.
ind.basis: No onshore instrument. A NYMEX hedge is offshore, USD-denominated, and thin enough that a large Indian autocatalyst hedge would move the market against itself. Most Indian exposure is embedded inside imported catalyst assemblies, so the price risk arrives as a component cost, not a metal purchase - which makes it nearly impossible to hedge cleanly.
ind.note: Substitution toward platinum in petrol autocats is the real long-run mitigant, and it is an engineering decision, not a treasury one.

South African power availability and shaft closures
EV share gains, which erode the demand base structurally

copper.hook: The bottleneck metal of electrification, and one India stopped being self-sufficient in the day Tuticorin closed.

trade.venue: LME (global benchmark) · COMEX (US) · SHFE and INE (China) · MCX (India)
trade.bench: LME Copper 3-month forward
trade.terms: USD per tonne (LME); US cents per pound (COMEX); INR per kg (MCX)
trade.settle: LME physical delivery of warehouse warrants on the prompt date; most OTC swaps cash-settle against the LME official cash price. MCX cash-settled against LME.
trade.curve: Modest contango in surplus years, flipping to sharp backwardation when LME stocks run low; the cash-to-3s spread is the standard tightness gauge
trade.liq: Deepest base metal across the three global venues; the usual macro vehicle for a China or electrification view

ind.contract: MCX Copper - 1 t lot, INR per kg, cash-settled against LME
ind.basis: MCX tracks LME converted at USDINR plus import duty and local premium. Because settlement references LME, the INR contract bundles metal risk and currency risk into one instrument - convenient for a physical buyer, but it means a treasurer who has already hedged USDINR separately is double-counting. Untangling that is a common first finding in a hedge-policy review.
ind.note: India has been a net importer since the 2018 Sterlite Tuticorin closure removed roughly 40% of domestic smelting. Hindalco and Hindustan Copper are the offsetting long positions.

drv: Chinese credit impulse and construction, still the biggest swing factor

copper.concWhy: Mine supply is only moderately concentrated, but China refines ~44% of world copper - the chokepoint is smelting, not mining, and mine HHI misses it

alum.hook: Congealed electricity. India smelts it competitively only because the smelters sit next to captive coal.

trade.bench: LME Aluminium 3-month, plus regional physical premia (Midwest, Rotterdam, MJP)
trade.terms: USD per tonne; INR per kg on MCX
trade.settle: LME warrant delivery; MCX cash-settled against LME
trade.curve: Persistent contango historically, financed by the carry trade; premia are a separate and separately volatile market
trade.liq: Deep on LME and SHFE; the physical premium leg is OTC and much thinner

ind.contract: MCX Aluminium (1 t) and Aluminium Mini
ind.basis: The LME contract hedges the metal but not the regional physical premium, which is a distinct exposure and moved violently through the 2025 tariff cycle. For an Indian smelter the bigger point is that aluminium risk is really power risk: at roughly 14 MWh per tonne, coal and grid tariffs drive the cost line more than the LME does.
ind.note: India is a net exporter of primary aluminium. Hindalco, Vedanta and NALCO are long the price - an aluminium spike is a P&L gain, not a cost.

Chinese smelting capacity cap of roughly 45 Mt

ironore.hook: The largest dry bulk trade on earth, and one of the few major inputs India does not have to import.

trade.bench: Platts IODEX 62% Fe CFR China; SGX TSI 62% Fe future
trade.terms: USD per dry metric tonne CFR China
trade.settle: Cash-settled against the monthly average index
trade.curve: Backwardated most of the time; the market rarely pays to carry ore
trade.liq: SGX is deeply liquid and the reference for seaborne hedging; DCE is the onshore Chinese pool

ind.contract: NCDEX has listed iron ore contracts with limited traction; SGX is the practical venue
ind.basis: The liquid benchmark prices 62% Fe CFR China. Indian domestic ore is sold at NMDC administered prices or through state auctions, and the correlation to CFR China is loose - a Chinese-index hedge against an Odisha purchase carries large basis. For most Indian mills the real exposure is domestic royalty, auction premia and evacuation logistics, none of which is hedgeable.
ind.note: India is ore-sufficient and a periodic exporter. Export duty policy is the swing variable: the May 2022 duty and its November 2022 rollback each moved domestic prices more than the seaborne index did.

steel.hook: India is the world's second-largest producer and, since 2024, a net importer - which changed who carries the price risk.

trade.venue: CME (US HRC) · LME (steel scrap, rebar) · SHFE · NCDEX (India, thin)
trade.bench: CME US Midwest HRC; Platts HRC FOB China and CFR India assessments
trade.terms: USD per short ton (CME); INR per tonne domestically
trade.settle: Cash-settled against the published index
trade.curve: Follows the steel spread - ore plus coking coal versus finished price
trade.liq: CME HRC is genuinely liquid for US exposure; Asian and Indian steel hedging is thin and mostly OTC

ind.contract: NCDEX steel contracts exist but carry negligible open interest; no usable onshore hedge
ind.basis: This is the largest hedging gap in Indian industry. A construction or auto client buying HRC in Mumbai has no liquid domestic contract, and the CME contract prices US Midwest steel - a different continent's supply-demand balance. The workable structures are contractual: escalation clauses indexed to a published assessment, or a synthetic spread hedge using iron ore (SGX) and coking coal (SGX) on the input side. Designing that synthetic is real advisory work.
ind.note: Safeguard duties, the EU CBAM on exports, and US Section 232 all bear on the same tonne. Tata Steel and JSW are long the price; L&T, autos and appliance makers are short it.

drv: Chinese output discipline and export volumes, the single biggest global variable

eua.hook: The price Indian steel and aluminium exporters started paying for their emissions on 1 January 2026.

trade.bench: ICE EUA December future
trade.settle: Physical delivery of allowances into a Union Registry account
trade.curve: Contango reflecting the cost of carry; the December contract is the liquidity point

ind.contract: No Indian contract. ICE Endex, EUR-denominated.
ind.basis: This is a new and genuinely hedgeable exposure that Indian exporters acquired by regulation rather than by choice. Under the CBAM definitive regime, an Indian steel or aluminium exporter to the EU must surrender certificates priced off the EU ETS, so the company now has a EUR-denominated carbon cost with a liquid futures market against it. Two subtleties matter: CBAM certificates for 2027 purchase are priced off the 2026 quarterly-average ETS price, not spot, so the correct hedge is an average-price structure rather than a simple future; and the exposure is EUR, so the currency leg goes into EUR rather than the usual USD - a different conversation with the bank and a different RBI permission profile. The Omnibus package cut the quarterly certificate-holding requirement from 80% to 50%, which relieves working capital but does not change the price exposure.
ind.note: Tata Steel, JSW Steel, Hindalco, JSPL and any Indian exporter of in-scope goods (iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen, electricity). First surrender is due 30 September 2027 for 2026 emissions.

ind.contract: Traded on Indian power exchanges under the CCTS compliance mechanism
ind.basis: This is the exposure most Indian industrial clients do not yet have on their risk register. The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme sets greenhouse gas intensity targets for obligated entities in aluminium, cement, pulp and paper, chlor-alkali, iron and steel, textiles, petrochemicals, petroleum refineries and fertiliser. Miss the target and you buy certificates; beat it and you sell them. It is an emerging INR-denominated commodity position sitting inside a manufacturing P&L, and the market is too new for a reliable price history - which means no VaR, no hedge, and a genuine need for scenario work instead. For a client already modelling CBAM, the natural question is whether an Indian carbon price paid domestically can be credited against the EU certificate obligation, which is a live policy question worth tracking.
ind.note: Obligated sectors overlap almost exactly with the CBAM in-scope list, which is not a coincidence. Compliance targets and the trading cycle are set by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency.
